actualProfiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
actualProfiles.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
actualProfiles.profile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
actualProfiles.topics: value of different knowledge types; ethically orientate oneself; enhance critical thinking; first-year requirement; societal partners; personal

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Economics
actualProfiles.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
actualProfiles.profile: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
actualProfiles.topics: game theory; theory of consumer behaviour; theory of the firm; market structure; aggregate output; inflation rate

actualProfiles.name: International Macroeconomics
actualProfiles.description2: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
actualProfiles.profile: This course explores the economy as a whole by examining its dynamics over the short, medium, and long run. Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.
actualProfiles.topics: national income; economic growth; unemployment are studied; business cycles; economic crises; international trade

actualProfiles.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
actualProfiles.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
actualProfiles.profile: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of advanced topics in microeconomic theory. Structured in three parts, the course begins with an in-depth analysis of consumer behaviour, including decision-making under uncertainty, non -egoistic preferences, and cognitive limitations. The second part analyses market structures with an emphasis on imperfect competition, strategic behaviour, and the functioning of factor markets. The final part of the course covers general equilibrium and market efficiency, investigating externalities and the role of government in the economy. Throughout the course, students will engage with research papers through presentations and discussions, bridging theoretical concepts with empirical evidence.
actualProfiles.topics: decision-making under uncertainty; non -egoistic preferences; cognitive limitations; general equilibrium; market efficiency; investigating externalities

actualProfiles.name: Public Economics
actualProfiles.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
actualProfiles.profile: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
actualProfiles.topics: market failure; public goods; p ublic spending; political economy; affect societal welfare; policies affect societal

actualProfiles.name: Econometrics
actualProfiles.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
actualProfiles.profile: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
actualProfiles.topics: monte carlo simulations; econometrics; tests t-test; instrumental variables; sampling distribution; estimators ordinary
actualProfiles.methods: Econometrics; Regression analysis; Instrumental variables; Hypothesis testing; Monte Carlo simulation; Stata

actualProfiles.name: Research Methods & Statistics
actualProfiles.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
actualProfiles.profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
actualProfiles.topics: research design; operationalization; sampling; experiments; surveys; descriptive and inferential statistics
actualProfiles.methods: Research design; Operationalization; Experimental design; Survey research; Sampling; Descriptive statistics; Inferential statistics; ANOVA

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Data Science
actualProfiles.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
actualProfiles.profile: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
actualProfiles.topics: spatial data; text data; data visualization; datasets; cleaning; manipulation

actualProfiles.name: Machine Learning
actualProfiles.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
actualProfiles.profile: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
actualProfiles.topics: linear regression; resampling methods; shrinkage approaches; tree - based methods; support vector machines; advanced tree based

actualProfiles.name: Law, Society & Justice
actualProfiles.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
actualProfiles.profile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
actualProfiles.topics: property law; torts law; moot court session; international legal organisations; legal traditions; socio scientific

actualProfiles.name: Modern History
actualProfiles.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
actualProfiles.profile: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.
actualProfiles.topics: national self determination; popular sovereignty; chronological overview; covers major economic; cultural developments; history

actualProfiles.name: History of Empires
actualProfiles.description2: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
actualProfiles.profile: This course is about great powers, superpowers and even hyperpowers. ‘Empire’ is a powerful and dangerous word. It has a rich and ambiguous history and strong polemical connotations now and in the past. The typical empire is usually presented as oppressive and ruthless, although some of the modern empires are democracies that focus upon the improvements of its society. This course deals with some of the most important empires in World History. Next to this some of the most important theories on empires will be treated. How is the rise and fall of empires explained? What are the sources of empire and how are great power politics conducted?
actualProfiles.topics: empires; major historical examples; benevolent features; discusses oppressive; power politics; contested

actualProfiles.name: Western Way of War
actualProfiles.description2: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
actualProfiles.profile: This course gives a chronological overview of the history of Warfare in the Western World from antiquity to the present day. All aspects of war on land, sea, and in the air are covered: weapons and technology; strategy and tactics; discipline and intelligence; mercenaries and standing armies; cavalry and infantry; chivalry and Blitzkrieg; guerrilla assault and nuclear arsenals. The central controversial thesis of this course is that war in western societies has followed a unique path leading to the Western hegemony of the world. From Greek hoplites, Roman legionnaires to the jet plane and cruise missile, war has served as the driving force behind the West’s rise to global domination. The history of the West, both at home and overseas, has centred around ferocious competition for mastery among uncompromisingly ambitious powers, in which the ruthless, innovative, and the decisive displaced the complacent, the imitative, and the irresolute.
actualProfiles.topics: illustrating competition; guerrilla warfare; nuclear arsenals; western; chronological overview; covers weapons

actualProfiles.name: History Research Seminar
actualProfiles.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
actualProfiles.profile: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.
actualProfiles.topics: many foreign troops like irish; emphasises methodological rigour; substantial research paper; interdisciplinary thinking; engaging critically; historical inquiry

actualProfiles.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
actualProfiles.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
actualProfiles.profile: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
actualProfiles.topics: human rights; french declaration; rights treaties; modern philosophers; traces; classical

actualProfiles.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
actualProfiles.description2: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
actualProfiles.profile: This course provides students insights into the main legal issues in the fields of criminal law and criminal justice. We will discuss the concepts of criminal accountability, differentiated types of ‘guilt’, the essentials of justifications and excuse, the importance of the legality principle and other fundamental considerations, such as the ‘presumption of innocence’. Students are also introduced to interdisciplinary research into organized crime. The main guiding principles of criminal law and criminal justice will be presented and investigated and the moral and legal debate on the justification of punishment and on recent developments in criminal law will be considered. Special attention will be paid to legal skills, such as reading legal texts, analyzing criminal case law and formulating a normative opinion, based on legally and morally sound argumentation. Students apply theory and skills in a simulated legal aid clinic.
actualProfiles.topics: ‘presumption of innocence’; reading legal texts; analyzing criminal case law; formulating a normative opinion; based on legally; morally sound argumentation

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Public International Law
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
actualProfiles.profile: This course serves as a general introduction to public international law as a field of study and professional discipline. Designed to provide you with a foundational knowledge of the creation and the historical evolution of the subject, it is broadly divided into three parts. The first part deals with general principles of international law such as its sources, subjects, and organization. In the second part, the focus shifts to specific domains, namely the regulation of the use of force, the law of armed co nflict, international criminal law, refugee law, and environmental law. The final part addresses the politics of international law as it delves into issues such as the right to self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law, and questions of treaty negotiation, compliance and effectiveness. The general purpose of the course is to shed light on some of the most important questions of international law both from a formal legal and a social science perspective. Performance in the course will be assessed through in-class exercises, a preparatory and an open book exam, a podcast and a reflection report.
actualProfiles.topics: its sources; right to self-determination; third world approaches to international law; questions of treaty negotiation; public international law; podcast connecting law

actualProfiles.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
actualProfiles.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
actualProfiles.profile: In this course on constitutional law and administrative law, students will undertake an exploration of the essential principles of these foundational legal fields. A comparative approach is used, examining and analyzing the constitutional law of five different legal systems. A constitution is the “fundamental and organic law of a nation or state that establishes the institutions and apparatus of government, defines the scope of governmental sovereign powers, and guarantees individual civil rights and civil liberties”, and ther efore, constitutional law is the “field of law dealing with aspects of constitutional provisions, such as restrictions on government powers and guarantees of rights.” (Blacks Law Dictionary 8 Ed, Garner et al eds, West 2004.) Yet, constitutional law is so much more than is suggested by these definitions. At the center of the modern constitutional state is the law, which protects peace, freedom and security. It is this law that is controlling, not the human actors in a state. In order that all may have acce ss to and rely on it, this law should be enshrined in a written document. Democracy demands a law that is enacted by a legislative body after public debate about its contents. The foundational values of a legal culture are written down in its constitution. The constitution takes up established values, tried and tested institutions and reliable political experience and passes them on to the next generation in a binding manner.
actualProfiles.topics: restrictions on government powers; guarantees of rights; constitutional law; comparative; religious constitutions; judicial review

actualProfiles.name: Foundations of European Union Law
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
actualProfiles.profile: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method.
actualProfiles.topics: different national laws throughout the eu; problem based exercises; internal market; guest lectures; legal order; framework

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
actualProfiles.profile: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science.
actualProfiles.topics: political philosophy; emphasises essay writing; contemporary texts; presentations; poverty; pluralism

actualProfiles.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
actualProfiles.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
actualProfiles.profile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
actualProfiles.topics: decline of political parties; impact of globalization; non majoritarian institutions; phenomena like democratic; like democratic backsliding; compare political systems

actualProfiles.name: Theory of International Relations
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
actualProfiles.profile: Brewing wars in the South China Sea, the Middle East, and Europe, trade wars, global climate change, amongst a plethora of other crises and difficulties, show the importance of understanding International Relations and geopolitics. This course gives the student a basic understanding of International Relations through a historical and contemporary scope. You work with a textbook to understand the different schools of thought within International Relations and then use historical or contemporary topics to apply these theories to. This will be achieved by group presentations. Your knowledge will be further increased by homework assignments and an exam. Finally, you end the course with a United Nations Security Council Simulation, where you take on the role of one of the UNSC members, and plead your country’s case in a current problem of international relations.
actualProfiles.topics: security council negotiation; council negotiation simulation; humanitarian intervention; south-south actors; global crises; international

actualProfiles.name: European Union Politics
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
actualProfiles.profile: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
actualProfiles.topics: decision making rules; outlines actors; politics; policy making; employs; responses

actualProfiles.name: Peace & Conflict
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
actualProfiles.profile: Peace and Conflict Studies is an interdisciplinary field that explores the causes, consequences, and potential solutions to both violent and nonviolent conflicts. Its goal is to understand the complex factors that contribute to conflict, the dynamics of violence, and the strategies for achieving lasting peace. The field encompasses insights from history, sociology, political science, international relations, and law, among other disciplines . This course introduces the field by examining and assessing multi ple theories of conflict and peacebuilding in the context of ongoing and past conflicts at regional, national and international levels. Peace and Conflict Studies is not only interdisciplinary but also shaped by diverse analytical perspectives. Some approaches emphasize structural inequality , clashing ideologies, and others focus on humiliation, historical wounds, and identity -based grievances, particularly in colonial or postcolonial contexts. Each lens draws attention to different forms of evidence and different peacebuilding strategies. As a result, this course demonstrates the importance of adopting a holistic approach that includes in ternational, institutional, and state -led elements, as well as cultural, interpersonal, and bottom-up actions led by civil society. The course uses “Travelling Concepts” as a tool for critically applying an interdisciplinary perspective. Students will compare how “justice,” “truth,” or “reconciliation” are mobilized in legal vs.
actualProfiles.topics: peace conflict; analyzes conflict causation; conflict transformation models; violence typologies; reconciliation; radicalisation

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Sociology
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
actualProfiles.profile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
actualProfiles.topics: those by marx; du bois; authors like marx; socio historical context; encourages exploration; social problems related

actualProfiles.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
actualProfiles.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
actualProfiles.profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.

actualProfiles.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
actualProfiles.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
actualProfiles.profile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. actualProfiles.name: Persuasive Communication
actualProfiles.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
actualProfiles.profile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
